name: Mongolian (Khalkha)
variety: Khalkha (Halh) Mongolian of Ulaanbaatar, Cyrillic script
sources: Svantesson, Jan-Olof; Tsendina, Anna; Karlsson, Anastasia & Franzén, Vivan (2005). The Phonology of Mongolian. Oxford University Press.
Karlsson, Anastasia (2005). Rhythm and Intonation in Halh Mongolian. Lund University.
Karlsson, Anastasia (2014). The intonational phonology of Mongolian. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology II. Oxford University Press.
Walker, Rachel (1997). Mongolian stress, licensing, and factorial typology. Manuscript, Rutgers Optimality Archive.
Nevins, Andrew (2009). Review of The Phonology of Mongolian. Phonology 26(3), 525-534.
contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated obstruents, both voiceless: /pʰ tʰ tsʰ tʃʰ/ (п т ц ч) versus /p t ts tʃ/ (б д з ж); there is no voicing contrast and no native /k/
pharyngeal (retracted tongue root) vowels /a ɔ ʊ/ versus non-pharyngeal /e o u/, with neutral /i/; ө and ү are the back or central rounded vowels /o u/, not front rounded vowels
long versus short vowels, in word-initial syllables only
full versus reduced (epenthetic, schwa-like) vowels in non-initial syllables
plain versus palatalised consonants, in pharyngeal words (spelt with ь or a following и or iotated vowel)
velar /ɡ/ versus uvular /ɢ/ at the end of pharyngeal stems (баг 'team' versus бага 'small')
alveolar /n/ versus velar /ŋ/ at the end of a syllable (хана 'wall' with /n/ versus хан with /ŋ/)
allophony: aspirated stops and affricates are post-aspirated word-initially and pre-aspirated after a vowel or sonorant, with devoicing of the end of the preceding vowel or sonorant
unaspirated /p t ts tʃ/ are plain voiceless stops and affricates that may be voiced between voiced sounds; /ɡ ɢ/ are voiced, and between vowels /ɢ/ is a fricative [ʁ] and /ɡ/ is [ɣ]
/ɮ/ is a voiced lateral fricative, devoiced to [ɬ] before aspirated consonants and often word-finally; there is no plain /l/
/x/ is velar in non-pharyngeal words and uvular [χ] in pharyngeal words; /ŋ/ likewise has a uvular variant
/n/ is [ŋ] at the end of a word and before velars; it is [n] again when resyllabified before a vowel
/w/ is a bilabial approximant or fricative [β], voiceless [ɸ] before voiceless consonants; /p/ occurs mainly word-initially and after /m w ɮ/
/r/ is a trill, devoiced word-finally and before voiceless consonants
reduced vowels are centralised copies of the vowel of the preceding syllable, [i]-like after palatalised and palato-alveolar consonants
pharyngeal vowels have a higher first formant than their non-pharyngeal partners; /i/ is slightly lower in pharyngeal words
short /e/ is merging with /i/ for many Ulaanbaatar speakers, and short /o/ is close and central [ɵ]
written final short vowels after н and г are not pronounced: they show that the consonant is /n/ rather than /ŋ/, or uvular /ɢ/ rather than velar /ɡ/
phonotactics: no onset clusters; loans get a copy vowel or an initial /i/ (спирт > испирт)
codas of two or three consonants are allowed if sonority falls; otherwise a schwa-like vowel is inserted as far to the left as possible, so the place of the reduced vowels is predictable
/ŋ w ɮ/ and /r/ do not begin native words; /ŋ/ cannot begin a syllable
pharyngeal harmony: all vowels of a word are pharyngeal /a ɔ ʊ/ or non-pharyngeal /e o u/; /i/ is transparent; a word with only /i/ is non-pharyngeal
rounding harmony among the non-high vowels: after /ɔ/ or /o/ a non-high suffix vowel is /ɔ/ or /o/; the high rounded vowels /ʊ u/ block it and /i/ is transparent
palatalised consonants occur only in pharyngeal words
minimal word is bimoraic (a long vowel, a diphthong or a closed syllable)

stress.type: non-contrastive and disputed; no lexical stress according to Svantesson et al. (2005) and Karlsson (2005)
stress.rule: A common rule (Walker 1997) puts stress on the rightmost heavy syllable (long vowel or diphthong) that is not word-final, otherwise on the only heavy syllable, otherwise on the first syllable; most native scholars describe first-syllable stress.
stress.cues: no consistent acoustic correlate of word stress; prominence comes from the full quality and length of the first-syllable vowel and from a phrase-initial pitch rise

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: short vowels of non-initial syllables are reduced to short centralised vowels, often devoiced or lost, and their place is predictable from syllable structure
rhythm.notes: Heavy consonant clusters and reduced vowels give a stress-timed impression although there is no lexical stress; the mora is the unit of tonal alignment (Karlsson 2005).

length.notes: Svantesson et al. (2005) report that in initial syllables a long vowel is about 208% as long as a short one; in non-initial syllables the full vowels (written double) are only about 127% and the reduced vowels about 71% of the length of an initial short vowel. Non-initial written long vowels are therefore phonologically short full vowels.

intonation.declarative: every prosodic word except the last begins with a rise (low on the first mora, high on the second); peaks step down through the utterance; final low
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by a clause-final particle (уу/үү, юу/юү); the final word may carry a high boundary tone instead of the final low
intonation.wh_question: marked by the particle вэ/бэ and the question word; ends low like a statement
intonation.continuation: high boundary at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: LH associated with the first two morae of the word: a long first vowel carries the whole rise, a short first vowel carries only the low and the high falls on the next mora
intonation.notes: After Karlsson (2005, 2014). Focus is marked by phrasing and by a raised initial rise, not by a pitch accent on a stressed syllable. The question and continuation entries are low confidence.

tone.notes: No lexical tone. The post-lexical LH rise that marks the left edge of each prosodic word is aligned with the first two morae (Karlsson 2005).

phonation: pre-aspirated stops and affricates after vowels, with breathy or voiceless end of the preceding vowel
lateral fricative /ɮ/ devoiced to [ɬ] next to voiceless sounds
devoicing or loss of reduced vowels between voiceless consonants

problems: the aspiration contrast is rendered as a voicing contrast: б д г ж are voiced [b d ɡ dʒ] and п т к ч are aspirated; Khalkha has voiceless unaspirated versus aspirated consonants, and there is no pre-aspiration after vowels
з is the voiced fricative [z]; Khalkha has the unaspirated affricate [ts] against aspirated ц [tsʰ]
л uses the ordinary lateral approximant formants although the table calls it a lateral fricative; [ɮ] and its voiceless variant [ɬ] are not produced

short vowels of non-initial syllables keep their written quality and are only shortened (length 100 against 150); in Khalkha they are schwa-like and predictable, and the final vowel letters of words such as хана and бага are silent
non-initial long vowels get the full long length (250-270), although they are only slightly longer than an initial short vowel in Khalkha
palatalised consonants are missing: ь is dropped (тавь sounds like тав, хонь like хон) or becomes a full [i] in dictionary entries (морь gives [mɔri])
үй is mapped to the diphthong of уй [ʊi], which breaks the harmony (үйл, хүйтэн); е is always [je], also before ө (ерөнхий); юу is read as two short vowels
no velar versus uvular variants: г and х are always [ɡ] and [x]
ө and ү have nearly the same formant targets (F1 386 against 380 Hz, F2 741 against 691 Hz)
a very short pause is inserted between all words (word_gap 1), so words are never linked, and the word-initial LH rises are not modelled
the ipa strings of the table are not IPA (O, U, 8, and u for ү), so --ipa output is misleading
good: seven vowel qualities with their own formant files, seven long vowels and four diphthongs
first-syllable prominence, in line with the usual description
harmony follows from the spelling in most words

notes: The eSpeak NG voice file also sets pitch 80-140 Hz, speed 85, a slightly lowered F1 and breath settings. The consonant list includes /kʰ f/, which occur in loanwords only, and /pʰ/, which is rare in native words.
